Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it (routing saves 50–60%); cascading runs the cheap model and escalates only on a signal — and the whole technique lives or dies on whether that escalation signal is calibrated.
🗣️ Plain English (no jargon)

Most of your traffic is easy. A small fraction is hard. Running everything on your best model means paying top price for the easy majority; running everything on a cheap model means failing the hard tail.

Routing decides before generating which model to use — based on the request's features (task class, length, language, user tier, keywords, or a small classifier model). Cascading decides after generating: run cheap, check the result, and escalate to the big model if it looks wrong.

Both sound free and both have a trap. Routing's trap is that a mis-route is a silent quality regression: you don't get an error, you get a mediocre answer. Cascading's trap is that you need a reliable way to tell "the cheap model was wrong" — and if your confidence signal is uncalibrated, you either escalate everything (no saving) or escalate nothing (quality loss).

The rule that makes this work: never route on the model's own verbalised confidence alone. Use a calibrated score, a deterministic check (schema valid? unit tests pass? citation present?), or a trained router.
🧠 The analogy (what you'll actually remember)
A hospital triage desk.
A nurse (router) assigns urgency before the doctor sees you, using a protocol — not vibes.
Some patients go to a GP (cheap model), some straight to a specialist (frontier model).
Occasionally the GP says "this needs a specialist" and refers up (cascade escalation).
If triage is bad, the wrong patients sit in the GP queue (mis-route = silent quality loss).
If the GP refers everyone up, you've built an expensive queue with extra steps (uncalibrated confidence).
❓ Why this exists — the problem it solves

Model tiers differ in cost by 5–20× while differing in quality on easy tasks by almost nothing. That gap is the opportunity: if 70–80% of your traffic is easy, tiering captures most of the cost reduction while keeping quality where it matters.
What made routing practical in 2025–26:
Cheap models got good enough for classification, extraction, summarisation and format-following.
Schemas and constrained decoding made cheap-model output verifiably well-formed, giving a deterministic escalation signal.
Routers became trainable — you can learn "which of my models handles which of my requests" from preference data instead of hand-writing rules.
Gateways made routing a config change rather than an app change.

Reported effect: 50–60% cost reduction with quality held, when the router is calibrated and measured. Which is why the honest framing is: routing is a measurement technique first and an optimisation second.
What a good router needs
A labelled set with difficulty. You need examples where cheap-model output was actually worse — otherwise you're guessing.
A calibrated threshold, not a vibe. Choose τ so the escalation rate hits your target, and measure the quality/cost curve at several τ values.
Slices, not averages. Check that routing doesn't systematically degrade a language, a customer tier, or an edge case — that's where silent regressions hide.
A drift plan. Traffic changes; re-fit the router on a schedule and monitor escalation rate as a leading indicator.
A kill switch. If the router misbehaves, route everything to the safe model — a config flag, not a deploy.

Evolution: manual "use the cheap model here" (2023) → function-calling routers + gateways (2024) → trained routers + cascade papers (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT-type cascades) (2025) → routing as harness-level policy with per-step models and cost-aware scheduling (2026). Direction: routing moving from "which model" to "which model and effort budget, per step."

Pre-mortem: the top-3 causes of a routing failure: (1) shipped without measuring quality at the chosen threshold; (2) escalation signal based on the model's verbalised confidence; (3) no per-slice monitoring, so one cohort degraded invisibly for months.
🏭 Production reality (what teams actually ship, Sept 2026)

Default: forced-tool classifier or small trained router; cheap model as default tier; deterministic verifier driving escalation where one exists (schemas, tests, arithmetic); judge cascade only for subjective outputs; threshold calibrated to a 10–30% escalation rate; per-slice quality monitoring; config-level kill switch.
Config that works for 80% of cases: two tiers; route by task class + length + tenant tier; escalate on schema/verifier failure; alarm if escalation rate moves ±1.5× from baseline; re-fit quarterly.
Observability you must have: escalation rate over time, quality by route, cost per success by route, router overhead cost, judge–human agreement if a judge is used, and slice-level quality.
Security/tenancy: tenants may have contractual model restrictions — routing must respect them; keep the routing policy auditable and log the model actually used per request.

Cost shape: routing is the second-biggest cost lever after caching, and unlike caching it can hurt quality — so it's the lever that most needs a measurement discipline around it.
